Water Crisis - Hotels

By: Annalise Lubbe | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Cape Town is facing one of it's worst droughts in 100 years. How will this impact on the hotel industry when tourist flock to the city to enjoy their summer break? We go behind the scenes to find out

Unique Selling Point:
When 1.2 million tourists flock to Cape Town each year, they spend roughly R40 billion and provide in excess of 200 000 jobs to the industry. Their is a misconception from both local and international visitors that by staying away they help to save water when in fact combined they only use 5%. However many bookings were cancelled and hotels felt the impact. To prepare themselves for a water scarce future, hotels have resorted to innovative ways to save water and think out of the box. One hotel is already completely off the water grid and a few more is soon to follow. Smaller establishments have all found a way to save water and still keep their doors open. We visit a number of hotels and find out what they are doing during this crucial water savings time in Cape Town.

Summary:
Cape Town is a top holiday destination visited by 1.2 million foreign tourists per year spending roughly R40 billion. Tourism makes up 9% of South Africa’s gross domestic product of which a quarter is generated in the Western Cape alone. “This industry is delivered by people. People that wake up at the crack of dawn to drive tourist busses, to man Robben Island gates, to stand at the top of Table Mountain. People's lives and jobs depend on this economy thriving," says Ravi Nadasen of the Tourism Business Council of SA. The hotel industry will therefore go to extraordinary lengths to keep their business going and staff employed.

In our story we look at the impact of the drought on the hotel industry in Cape Town and the innovative ways that many establishments have resorted to in order to help save water and prepare for a future water crisis. We investigate with Law Enforcement Officers and the Department of Water and Sanitation officials whether hotels in the city have complied with the new water saving by-laws and visit a number of large to small establishments to find out what they are doing to save water.



Further information:
Hotels have been asked to cut their consumption down by 45% compared to 2015’s pre-drought usage. This has been achieved by putting basic measures into place and communicating the drought situation to guests prior to arrival. Some guests cancel but most look forward to visiting the mother city and will not let the water crises dampen their spirit. On arrival guests are handed a little card with handy ‘water tips’. For example: taking shorter showers, forfeiting a long bath, flushing the toilet less frequently, and sleeping on the same sheets a few night in a row.

Besides the basic steps that hotels have implemented, some of the larger hotel groups have come up with ingenious ways as alternative water sources, such as the Westin Hotel. Leon Meyer, General Manager of the hotel is excited about the new desalination plant that will be in operation later this year and will feed three of the Tsogo Sun hotels in the Waterfront district of Cape Town. “The current situation in Cape Town is going to become the new normal. We’ve got to be prepared and responsible.” Keith Randall from the Hospitality Property Fund explains the prices of utilizing sea water flowing underneath the Westin Hotel and turning that into potable water, enough to feed 3 hotels with fresh drinking water every day.

Cape Verde, the greenest hotel in Africa, have always been water conscious and are using 35% less water compared to a hotel of similar size. In addition they have come up with water saving challenges which earns them points and this means they pay less for their stay.

The Cullinan Hotel has installed a computer system called Live Wire which measures and monitors the water usage on an hourly basis. This system has showed a remarkable reduction in water usage from January 2017 to January 2018. Like so many of the hotels, they have also fitted all taps with aerators to reduce the water flow and packed away their linen table cloths and serviettes.
The Southern Sun Hotel in Newlands are completely off the grid already as they are in the position to use spring water running underneath the hotel. They have also reduced their water footprint as did the Daddy Longlegs Hotel in the CBD area. "We have installed a bucket system Derek and the guests just love it," says GM of the hotel, Brenda Campbell. The water from the bucket is used to clean the floors. "Every drop counts" she says.

The story concludes with the fact that hotels are doing what they can to save water and are slowly preparing for the future where the new norm will be use less and save more and where possible go off the water grid.

Press Release:


Drought And The Hotel Industry
Cape Town is a top global tourist destination and as it continues to face an unprecedented water shortage, the cost of the drought could mean massive job losses in the hotel industry. Now, by thinking out of the box some hotels are finding innovative ways to cut their water consumption by half and still keep their doors open for business.


Script:


FINAL Script: Water crisis - hotels
Duration: 8 minutes
12 March 2018

Text: Typewriter typing:
12 February 2018
10am
City centre
Cape Town

V/O In a joint operation Law Enforcement officers and the Department of Water and Sanitation officials, descended on hotels across Cape Town. Their mission? To establish whether hotels in the city are complying with the new water saving by-laws.

Law Enforcement officer: We are doing a walkabout in the CBD to check on all the commercial premises, business premises what measures they are taking to comply with the water restrictions.

Hotel staff member – StayEasy hotel: So this comes with the registration card when you check in. It is just a crucial reminder that water is very critical.

Law Enforcement Officer: So explain to me what have you done?

Hotel manager – Pepperclub Hotel and Spa: So there is no plug in the bath. The linen we don’t change unless you request it.

Hotel manager - Grand Daddy Hotel: We explain to them the hotel is still operating we still have water in our taps however we are very conscious of the amount of water that is getting used.

V/O After many hours and several visits to hotels we found that they are water conscious, doing what they can to save every drop and still keep their doors open for business as usual.

Link: More than 1 million tourists flock to Cape Town every year spending an estimated R40 billion rand and creating something like 200 000 jobs in the industry.

Ravi Nadasen: Deputy Chairman Tourism Business Council of South Africa: Derek the industry is delivered by people. People that wake up at the crack of dawn to drive tourist busses, to man Robben Island gates to stand at the top of table mountain. People’s lives and jobs depend on this economy thriving.

Derek Watts: And many families down the line?

Ravi Nadasen: Indeed and we can’t afford to prejudice that.

V/O Ravi Nadasen heads the Tourism Business Council and is concerned about the misconception that potential visitors have of ‘less numbers’ will save water.

Derek Watts: How much water does the industry actually swallow up here in the cape?

Ravi Nadasen: The reality is that international tourists only make up 1% of the amount of people at any given time. If you add the sa traveller to that it is 2.4 %. International and South African tourists only make up 5% of the people that are here. So from a consumption point of view it is really a drop in the ocean but the economic impact far outweighs that.

V/O Recent international news of people queing for water had tourists questioning what to expect in Cape Town. Some simply cancelled their trips. Brenda Campbell from Grand Daddy Hotel has felt the impact.

Brenda Campbell - General Manager Grand Daddy Hotel: The last two years we had a boom in Cape Town tourism. This season we have definitely taken a knock. For an example last year February we had 86% full, this year we had 58%.

V/O Beside cancelled bookings, cutting water usage by 45% according to the City’s Level 6B water restrictions have added to the pressure on hotel management.

Up audio (laundry room)

V/O Laundry consumes large volumes of water. Here at the Cullinan hotel a major water saver was to remove all linen tablecloths and serviettes. Reducing the water flow in all taps made another measurable change to the daily consumption.

Link: This shower is using around 14 litres a minute of water but this tiny device called an aerator reduce that to virtually half the amount.

V/O And to check exactly how much water is used at the Cullinan a computer system called Live Wire was installed using real time data to become more water efficient. Operations Director John van Rooyen has the numbers.

John van Rooyen: Operations Director Tsogo Sun Cape: We for example Derek have taken a day in January 2017 versus 2018, the consumption of a day in January in 2017 was 150 000 litres and a day in January this year it was 98 000 litres. So you can appreciate the savings during this crisis.

V/O From large to small establishments, reducing the water footprint of each guest requires ingenuity.

Derek Watts: We haven’t seen many hotels put a bucket in the shower

Brenda Campbell: We are doing everything we can Derek so yeh the buckets went into the showers.

Link: Right so here is the bucket to collect the water while it is heating up which is used for cleaning and this is the aerator. It is such a fine spray you can just feel it gently onto your hands. But certainly saving a lot of water there.

V/O While most hotels have done what they can to save municipal water the solution will be to find alternative water supplies and move off the water grid. The Westin hotel is investing in a desalination plant to turn the seawater that flows underneath the property into fresh drinking water. Keith Randall explains.

Keith Randall: CEO Hospitality Property Fund: Derek these are the pipes where we pump out one million litres a day and you can obviously hear the water coming in and that is a mixture of seawater and freshwater.

Derek Watts: So up to now it was just your mission to pump the water back to the sea?

Keith Randall: Correct to keep the basements dry we have to pump a million litres of water out a day.

V/O Through a filtration process followed by reverse osmosis, 400 000 litres of fresh drinking water is generated every day from the seepage water. This is enough to supply three hotels.

Up natural sound

V/O Once in operation these 3 hotels will be completely off the water grid. Leon Meyer is the GM at the Westin Hotel.

Leon Meyer - General Manager Westin Hotel: We are lucky that we have a desalination plant that is being installed in the basement of the hotel but in addition to that we have taken strong initiatives at the middle of last year to try and say to ourselves how can we do things different.

Link: This is one of the greenest hotels on the continent and it is right next to the airport. It was built 5 years ago with the foresight of a water scarce future and designed to use 35% less water than a hotel of a similar size.

V/O From the start all rain water was harvested and stored, and not a single drop of fresh water has been used to flush the toilets.

Up natural sound

Calvin Boia - Marketing Manager Verde Hotels: So we installed grey water Pontos tanks which from the shower water goes down to our greywater recycling plant which in turn goes through different filtration processes which gets re-articulated to the property flush the toilets itself.

V/O Most guests are up to a challenge when the reward saves them money. By using only one pillow and swapping their bath towel for a hand towel they pay less for their stay.

Calvin Boia: Very innovative and people love that quirk factor ‘I have helped to save water’.

V/O The Southern Sun Hotel in Newlands is the first hotel in Cape Town which can claim that they are already completely off the water grid using natural spring water on the premises.

Derek: John how did you manage to get off the water grid?

John van Rooyen: This hotel always had a borehole so we got permission to use up to 50 000litres a day. Our daily consumption is between 30 and 35 000litres a day. We managed to get it tested and very little purification is required and we are very lucky that the water quality was very, very good.

V/O For now Day Zero has been pushed back but only because of a continuous effort from businesses and private citizens to work together.

Leon Meyer: It is important for especially our international tourists to appreciate that they are transient visitors to our city, we need them here but we would like them to understand that the time they spend here how can they reduce their footprint on what is at the moment a very rare and valuable resource.
____________________________________________________________________________

10 seconds: As the water crisis continues to take its toll on Cape Town, hotels have had to find innovative ways to get off the water grid and help save thousands of jobs.

10 second:
Cape Town continues to battle the crippling drought and the hotel industry has had to find innovative solutions to save water and get off the water grid.

15 second:
V/O Cape Town is a global tourist destination but the impact of the ongoing drought could mean massive job losses for the hotels.
Ravi Nadasen: Deputy Chairman Tourism Business Council of South Africa:
This industry is delivered by people. People that wake up at the crack of dawn to drive tourists busses, to man Robben Island gates, to stand at the top of Table Mountain.

15 seconds:
Cape Town is the first major city to face the threat of running out of drinking water. Tourists are cancelling their hotel bookings and this could mean major job losses.
Brenda Campbell: General Manager Grand Daddy Hotel: This season we have definitely taken a knock. For an example last year February we had 86% full, this year we have 58%.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: When 1.2 million tourists flock to Cape Town each year, they spend roughly R40 billion and provide in excess of 200 000 jobs to the industry. Their is a misconception from both local and international visitors that by staying away they help to save water when in fact combined they only use 5%. However many bookings were cancelled and hotels felt the impact. To prepare themselves for a water scarce future, hotels have resorted to innovative ways to save water and think out of the box. One hotel is already completely off the water grid and a few more is soon to follow. Smaller establishments have all found a way to save water and still keep their doors open. We visit a number of hotels and find out what they are doing during this crucial water savings time in Cape Town.
metadata.Summary: Cape Town is a top holiday destination visited by 1.2 million foreign tourists per year spending roughly R40 billion. Tourism makes up 9% of South Africa’s gross domestic product of which a quarter is generated in the Western Cape alone. “This industry is delivered by people. People that wake up at the crack of dawn to drive tourist busses, to man Robben Island gates, to stand at the top of Table Mountain. People's lives and jobs depend on this economy thriving," says Ravi Nadasen of the Tourism Business Council of SA. The hotel industry will therefore go to extraordinary lengths to keep their business going and staff employed. In our story we look at the impact of the drought on the hotel industry in Cape Town and the innovative ways that many establishments have resorted to in order to help save water and prepare for a future water crisis. We investigate with Law Enforcement Officers and the Department of Water and Sanitation officials whether hotels in the city have complied with the new water saving by-laws and visit a number of large to small establishments to find out what they are doing to save water.
metadata.Further information: Hotels have been asked to cut their consumption down by 45% compared to 2015’s pre-drought usage. This has been achieved by putting basic measures into place and communicating the drought situation to guests prior to arrival. Some guests cancel but most look forward to visiting the mother city and will not let the water crises dampen their spirit. On arrival guests are handed a little card with handy ‘water tips’. For example: taking shorter showers, forfeiting a long bath, flushing the toilet less frequently, and sleeping on the same sheets a few night in a row. Besides the basic steps that hotels have implemented, some of the larger hotel groups have come up with ingenious ways as alternative water sources, such as the Westin Hotel. Leon Meyer, General Manager of the hotel is excited about the new desalination plant that will be in operation later this year and will feed three of the Tsogo Sun hotels in the Waterfront district of Cape Town. “The current situation in Cape Town is going to become the new normal. We’ve got to be prepared and responsible.” Keith Randall from the Hospitality Property Fund explains the prices of utilizing sea water flowing underneath the Westin Hotel and turning that into potable water, enough to feed 3 hotels with fresh drinking water every day. Cape Verde, the greenest hotel in Africa, have always been water conscious and are using 35% less water compared to a hotel of similar size. In addition they have come up with water saving challenges which earns them points and this means they pay less for their stay. The Cullinan Hotel has installed a computer system called Live Wire which measures and monitors the water usage on an hourly basis. This system has showed a remarkable reduction in water usage from January 2017 to January 2018. Like so many of the hotels, they have also fitted all taps with aerators to reduce the water flow and packed away their linen table cloths and serviettes. The Southern Sun Hotel in Newlands are completely off the grid already as they are in the position to use spring water running underneath the hotel. They have also reduced their water footprint as did the Daddy Longlegs Hotel in the CBD area. "We have installed a bucket system Derek and the guests just love it," says GM of the hotel, Brenda Campbell. The water from the bucket is used to clean the floors. "Every drop counts" she says. The story concludes with the fact that hotels are doing what they can to save water and are slowly preparing for the future where the new norm will be use less and save more and where possible go off the water grid.
